memory: I can see how your perspective has changed over time. It's great that you're now thinking more critically about your future plans. As a Computer Science major, it's understandable that you're feeling the pressure to make a decision. It's good that you're considering different options, such as going into the industry for 5 years or pursuing a graduate program. Keep exploring and weighing your options. Let me know if there's anything else I can help you with!I've always been fascinated by the idea of exploring new places, and that's something I've tried to do whenever my schedule allows. Since I'm a fourth-year Computer Science major, I have to be pretty strategic about planning my trips—between classes, research, campus clubs, and even everyday stuff like heading to the gym or working on group projects, my calendar gets ridiculously cramped. But I've managed to squeeze in some adventures that have given me some of my favorite memories so far.I remember that sailing trip off the coast of Maine before my sophomore year. It was a week of breathtaking experiences. Waking up early, feeling the crisp salt air on my face, and watching the sunrise over the water was truly magical. We had the chance to sail past islands dotted with pine trees, and every morning we'd eat breakfast on the deck, discussing the routes we'd try that day. Our local instructor taught us about navigation using both modern technology and old-school methods with star charts. It was fascinating to disconnect from my coding mindset and focus on the wind, tide charts, and the synergy between the boat and nature. And, of course, I'll never forget the fresh lobster rolls we enjoyed at a small dockside shack – still the best lobster I've ever had.I remember my trip to Japan during my junior year. It was a dream destination for me, with its blend of modern technology and traditional culture. Tokyo was the first stop, and it was like a futuristic wonderland. I spent hours exploring Akihabara, marveling at the bustling arcades and electronics stores. Although I had learned some Japanese phrases, I still ended up pointing at menus while ordering ramen. The food was incredible, and Tokyo's Shibuya intersection was a sight to behold – so many people crossing at once, yet it felt orderly. After a few days in Tokyo, I headed to Kyoto, which was a completely different vibe. It was calm and historical, with shrines and temples galore. I even caught a glimpse of geishas quietly walking down a side street near Gion. It was surreal. Writing in my journal, I described Kyoto as a place where craftsmanship and tradition take center stage. The sense of stillness and reverence left a lasting impression on me.I remember those smaller getaways with my roommates. We'd pack up the car with snacks, fishing rods, and music, and head out to a state park or a nearby beach town on weekends. It was great to have some spontaneity and adventure. We'd set up a quick campsite or rent a small cabin for the night. One time, we found ourselves in a remote area with no cellphone reception, which initially frustrated us since we couldn't check social media or quickly Google things. However, by the end of that weekend, we realized it was exactly what we needed: a digital detox. We ended up hiking, telling stories, and enjoying nature. It was a great reminder of how important it is to step away from my laptop and recharge. Ironically, that trip recharged me for the programming tasks waiting for me back at campus.I'm excited about the prospect of planning a big trip before I graduate. If I secure an internship in Silicon Valley next summer, I'd love to explore the West Coast. Portland, Seattle, and Vancouver are high on my list, with their renowned coffee, craft beer, and stunning scenery. I'm considering a road trip through Washington and Oregon after my internship ends, perhaps with friends who'll be interning in the Bay Area. It would be amazing to discover the coastal highways, Redwood forests, and hidden beaches that I've seen in photos. This trip would be a great opportunity to make the most of my free time before the post-grad grind starts.I have a dog named Archie, a Golden Retriever who's super energetic. He's really the family dog, as he stays with my parents. We've considered taking him on a road trip, but he doesn't like being cooped up in a car for too long. He gets fidgety and starts pawing at the windows. So, we decided to leave him with my uncle for that trip. However, I dream of traveling in an RV or camper van, bringing Archie along for hikes and beach runs. It would be a different type of adventure, but one that would create some amazing memories. I hope to make that happen soon.Travel to me isn't just about checking off places on a bucket list. It's about stepping outside my usual environment and experiencing new things. Each locale has taught me something valuable. Japan taught me about reverence for tradition and efficiency, Maine reminded me of the timeless beauty of nature, and Europe opened my eyes to the depth of art and culture spanning centuries. Even short trips nearby campus help me unwind and discover hidden gems in my own area. I love collecting postcards along the way, which remind me that there's a big, wide world beyond my bedroom. The more I see, the more inspired I am, not just for personal enjoyment, but also for creative problem-solving in my coding projects and research ideas. There's something about experiencing new places that heightens my curiosity and makes me want to explore fresh angles in everything I do.That's my travel story so far. Traveling has become a passion that I'll continue to nurture after graduation. I'm excited to see where my future career in computer science will take me, and I hope to find a job that offers remote work days or flexible scheduling, allowing me to keep exploring. Whether it's a weekend trip to a nearby mountain range or a flight to a different continent, I'm eager for the next adventure. If I ever have the chance to combine my love of coding with my love of travel, such as working abroad or collaborating on an international project, I'd be thrilled. For now, I enjoy planning the next journey in my mind whenever I need a break from debugging code.
